transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
In France, protesters clashed with police
and demonstrations around the country
over the cost of living.
These grew out of the student protests over schools.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley has more.
Today's nationwide protests are being called
a day of anger against what demonstrators say
are 10 years of austerity policies of Emmanuel Macron,
who they call a president of the ring.
French TV is showing early violence
in cities like Lyon and Marseille.
In Paris's Place de la République,
where most protest marches usually begin happily,
riot police are already shooting tear gas
at protesters throwing projectiles.
In Marseille, a hooded use broke into the town hall
using metal barricades as a battering ram.
A few left-wing politicians
who were to join the protest today
blamed the violence on weeks of police repression
of student protesters.
Analysts say there is a complete political fracture in France.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pierre News, Paris.
President Trump signed an executive order last night
waving new sanctions against Russia
that Congress just passed last month,
days before they would take effect.
Ukraine's President Zelensky says it helps Russia.
It follows last week's announcement of a deal
to import Russian diesel.
And Piers Ron Elving has more.
What was the Russia diesel deal really all about?
Why was it worth being seen
as aiding the Russian invaders of Ukraine,
worth being yoked with Vladimir Putin
as a dictator seeking his own enrichment?
Was it worth signing that executive order,
abandoning the Lindsey Graham Act,
a bipartisan set of sanctions on Russia?
All these things together seem to indicate
a clear shift away from backing Ukraine
to backing Putin and Russia
in this, their latest aggression and land grab.
And Piers Ron Elving, some Republicans aren't happy
about waving sanctions, including Congressman Don Bacon,
who says on social media Trump's prolonging the war,
not ending it.
The Trump administration is escalating its voter role fight
with California, even as voting is already underway
for the midterm elections.
And Piers Jew Joffee Block reports,
the Justice Department is now warning election officials
they could face charges.
Earlier this week, the Department of Justice
gave California and Los Angeles County just 48 hours
to review 20,000 registered voters,
federal officials had flagged as likely non-citizens.
The Justice Department demanded election officials
sequester those voters' ballots
if they couldn't prove the voters are US citizens.
California's Secretary of State argued
the demand was contrary to state and federal law,
and the DOJ sued.
In the latest escalation, a top DOJ official
sent a letter warning local officials
could be criminally liable if they process ballots
of people, federal agencies identified as non-citizens.
Yet previous Trump administration claims
about tallies of non-citizens on voter rolls
have been proven wrong.
Jew Joffee Block, NPR News.
- You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Groups around the country are holding
more than 3,000 No Kings vote early marches and events today,
trying to increase voter turnout
for the midterm elections next month.
It's a pivot for the No Kings Coalition,
comprised of hundreds of partner organizations
that previously focused on sending a message
about Trump's action in office.
Now, organizers say they're focused on voting
and getting people trained as poll watchers
head of the midterms that are just weeks away.
The rallies vary around the country.
In Washington, scores of people are gathering for March.
Indian police have detained the founder
of the popular youth group, Kakarosh Janta Party,
which has been campaigning for the resignation
of India's top election official.
NPR's Omkar Khandekar has more.
India's opposition parties and pressure groups
like Kokro Janta Party have demanded
that the election chief, Kyanesh Kumar, step down.
They accuse him of manipulation
in favor of the ruling BJP party
after the election commission deleted
more than 130 million names from India's voter rolls.
Hundreds gathered in Central Delhi,
defying police orders restricting protests.
They chanted slogans against the election commissioner
and the prime minister, even as the security forces
in dried gear tried to break up the crowd.
The Kokro Janta Party said police detained their founder
before he could join the demonstration.
Omkar Khandekar, NPR News, New Delhi.
And that party started as an online satire
attracting millions of followers.
I'm Janine Herbst, and you're listening
to NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: French nationwide protests over cost of living and Macron austerity turn violent in Paris, Lyon, Marseille
Trump signs executive order waiving Russia sanctions Congress passed, drawing Zelensky criticism over Russian diesel deal
Trump administration escalates California voter roll fight, warning local election officials of criminal liability over ballots
No Kings coalition holds over 3,000 events nationwide, shifting focus to midterm voter turnout and poll watching
Indian police detain founder of Gen Z youth group Kakarosh Janta Party amid protests against election chief Gyanesh Kumar
